Work ONLY inside /opt/nxeon-wt-leadgen4 (a pre-created git worktree, branch `feature/coldemail-leadgen4`, off the Nxeon hosting platform's main repo). Do NOT touch /opt/nxeon or any other /opt/nxeon-wt-* directory — two other agents are doing similar lead-research work in parallel right now on DIFFERENT niches (chamber-of-commerce directories nationwide, and gaming/esports/hosting businesses). Stay in your own lane described below to avoid duplicate work. `node_modules` and `.env` are symlinks to the main repo — NEVER `git add -A` (known hazard, can corrupt the main repo's real `node_modules`). Only `git add` exact file paths you changed.

## Context: a previous, smaller version of this exact task already ran successfully

A prior agent researched 3 niches (web/marketing agencies via 3 chamber directories, gaming cafes via 1 directory) and delivered 29 well-sourced B2B contacts, each with the exact source URL recorded — proper provenance was the whole point, since 3 EARLIER batches (1,709+2,681+4,221 contacts) had none at all and nobody could verify where they came from. The owner's reaction to 29: **"29 leads is not very good, we need hundreds, if not thousands."** Your job is to open up a THIRD niche entirely, complementary to the other two agents' work, to add real volume without duplicating their sources.

## Your lane: small e-commerce / online-business owners who plausibly need a VPS or dedicated server

Nxeon sells full-root NVMe VPS and dedicated servers (see `app/(marketing)/vps/` and `app/(marketing)/dedicated-servers/` or similar marketing pages for exact positioning) aimed partly at developers/small businesses running their own web apps, e-commerce stores, or SaaS products who've outgrown basic shared hosting. Good target categories to research (pick 2-4 and go deep rather than skimming many):
- Small, independent Shopify/WooCommerce store owners who publicly list needing more control/performance (check business directories or public app-marketplace developer/agency listings — e.g., a Shopify Plus partner agency directory, if one is openly browsable per its robots.txt).
- Independent SaaS/software makers or indie hackers who publicly list their own product's contact email on their own site (a "Contact" or "Support" page for a small, real, named product — not a personal blog or social profile).
- Freelance web developers / small dev shops (distinct from the marketing/design agencies the other agent is covering — look specifically for backend/full-stack developer directories or "hire a developer" public listings, if openly accessible).
- IT/managed-service-provider (MSP) small businesses, which often need VPS/dedicated capacity to host client workloads — many local business directories or MSP association member lists exist publicly.

For EVERY contact: visit the business's own website and confirm the email is genuinely published there (info@/contact@/support@/hello@, or a named role clearly tied to the business). Never trust a directory listing, aggregator, or search-result snippet alone — if you can't verify on the business's own page, drop that candidate.

Record, for every contact: business name, email, and the EXACT URL(s) where you found and verified it — non-negotiable, this is the entire point of the exercise.

## Explicitly OUT of scope — same rules as before, no exceptions

- No personal/consumer emails, no scraping individuals' social media profiles, no targeting private individuals (a solo freelancer's own published BUSINESS contact on their own professional site is fine; their personal Instagram is not).
- No bypassing paywalls, CAPTCHAs, login walls, or robots.txt/ToS restrictions. Check robots.txt before using any directory; skip and move on if disallowed.
- No purchasing or using any third-party list/data product — your own research via WebSearch/WebFetch against openly public sources only.
- Don't pad numbers with unverifiable contacts. An honest "checked N sources, verified M good contacts" beats a padded number — quality and real provenance matter more than volume here.

## Loading the data

Use the existing importer, exactly like the prior batch: `scripts/import-leads.ts` (wraps `lib/coldemail/import.ts` + `lib/coldemail/lead-store.ts`) with `--list "<descriptive name>" --create-list --consent --note "<how this batch was sourced>"`. Read `lib/coldemail/import.ts`'s `LeadRow`/`sourceUrl` handling first (added specifically for per-contact provenance) so each contact's source URL lands in its own `ConsentRecord.note`. This is a TEST/staging data-population exercise — no actual outbound send happens as a result of your work.

## Constraints — important

- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npm run build` inside `/opt/nxeon-wt-leadgen4` before finishing IF you touch any app code (unlikely).
- Commit any code changes (not the imported data, which lives in Postgres) with a clear message. Do NOT merge to main, do NOT touch staging, do NOT run deploy/promote scripts.
- Report back: which niches/sources you actually used (and any you skipped, and why), the real contact count, the `EmailList` name(s) and `ImportBatch.note` content, and confirm you committed any code changes on `feature/coldemail-leadgen4`.

content.text:
## Summary

Worked entirely inside `/opt/nxeon-wt-leadgen4` on `feature/coldemail-leadgen4`, no other worktree or repo touched.

**Niches researched** (2 of the 4 suggested, gone deep rather than skimming many, per instructions):

1. **Small dev shops / MSPs** — via GoodFirms.co's open, robots.txt-permitted company directory (`/companies/web-development-agency` pages 1–4, `/it-services/it-networking-companies` pages 1–2, `/it-services/it-consulting` pages 1–2). Pulled 310 company profile slugs, filtered to small teams (mostly 2–49 employees), then verified each candidate's email directly on the business's **own site** (mailto: links, schema.org ContactPoint/Organization emails, or visible footer/contact-page text) — 29 verified this way.
2. **Independent SaaS/indie makers** — via BetaList.com's homepage (open robots.txt), resolving each of the 55 listed startups' `/visit` redirect to the product's real domain, then confirming a genuinely published support/contact email on that product's own site — 16 verified (one dedup: two products from the same "Wiser5 LLC" business share one email).

**Skipped/dropped, and why:**
- Clutch.co, DesignRush, TheManifest, InfoMSP, LaunchingNext, IndieHackers, SaaSHub — all sit behind a Cloudflare JS challenge; skipped per the no-CAPTCHA-bypass rule.
- `mspcompanies.us` — looked promising (open robots.txt) but its own nav exposes `/email-list` and `/data-report` pages, marking it as a lead-data broker rather than a neutral directory; skipped per the no-third-party-data-product rule.
- SideProjectors — open robots.txt but fully client-rendered JS SPA, no server-rendered listing content to work from.
- Many individual GoodFirms candidates were found and then **dropped** because no email could be confirmed on their own site (form-only contact pages, JS-only homepages with nothing visible): e.g. AlpineRoot, 24/7 Techies, LLT Group, Ssquares Tech, DynaSoft, Zipnom, ICS NJ, KEYSS Inc, Fusion Technologies, AppMakers LA, Atlanta I.T. Service — quality bar enforced rather than padding the count.
- GoodFirms rate-limits aggressively; after the first ~16 fetches it started serving Cloudflare challenge pages. Ran two patient background retry passes (longer delays) to recover more, then stopped a third pass early once yield dropped to near zero rather than let it run indefinitely.

**Result:** 47 real, individually-sourced contacts imported via `scripts/import-leads.ts` (same tool/flow as the prior batch) into one `EmailList`: **"VPS/Dedicated prospects: small dev shops, MSPs & indie SaaS (batch 1)"**, across two `ImportBatch` runs (45 + a 2-contact top-up) with `--consent` and descriptive `--note` provenance on each batch, plus the exact source URL recorded per-contact in `ConsentRecord.note` (confirmed via a throwaway DB check script, since deleted). Verified in Postgres: 47 members in the list.

No application code was changed — only the existing importer was run against research CSVs in scratchpad — so `git status` in the worktree is clean and there is nothing to commit.
